source.excerpt: So, first of all, let me assert my firm belief that the only thing we have to fear is fear itself—nameless, unreasoning, unjustified terror which paralyzes needed efforts to convert retreat into advance.
source.cutTag: ↑ the famous version stops at “fear itself”
source.excerptNote: The slogan drops everything after the em-dash. FDR didn't mean fear in general — he named a specific “nameless, unreasoning, unjustified terror”: the public panic that was itself accelerating the collapse. The truncation is a lesson in how a phrase outlives its own qualifying clause.

trail: Exact wording confirmed against two independent full transcripts — Wikisource and Yale's Avalon Project — including the clause the slogan drops.
The delivery is preserved on audio at the Internet Archive (FDR even ad-libbed an opening line absent from his reading copy).
The drafting history — that the sentence was inserted by adviser Louis Howe, not in Raymond Moley's draft — is documented by the FDR Presidential Library and TeachingHistory.org.
The aphorism's older lineage (Montaigne, Bacon, Thoreau) is traced by Interesting Literature.

misattribution.heading: What people get wrong
misattribution.intro: The line is genuinely FDR's — he spoke it. But two things everyone assumes about it aren't true:

items.who: that FDR composed the phrase himself
items.why: The sentence wasn't in Raymond Moley's principal draft. It was inserted by FDR's longtime adviser Louis Howe; FDR then edited the tail, changing Howe's ending to “convert retreat into advance.” FDR Library ↗

items.who: that it was an original idea in 1933
items.why: The aphorism is centuries old: Montaigne (1580), Francis Bacon's “Nil terribile nisi ipse timor” (1623), and Thoreau (1851) all said versions of it. Howe's own immediate source is still debated. The literary lineage ↗

misattribution.truthLine: The bottom line: Roosevelt truly spoke it on March 4, 1933 — but the words were drafted by Louis Howe, and the idea runs from Montaigne to Thoreau. What FDR added was the delivery, at the exact moment a terrified country needed it. Who wrote the line ↗

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Roosevelt took office at the nadir of the Great Depression: a quarter of the workforce was unemployed, thousands of banks had failed, and a nationwide banking panic was underway the very morning of the inauguration. The line reframed the crisis as psychological as much as material — arguing that panic itself was accelerating the collapse — and set the confident, activist tone for the New Deal.
context.pull: A specific “nameless, unreasoning terror” — not fear in general.
detailsBody: Broadcast live to tens of millions, it became one of the most famous opening lines in American oratory and a template for presidential crisis rhetoric. Its truncation into a bare slogan is itself the lesson: memorable phrasing outlives the qualifying context that gave it precision.

Howe's assistant Lela Stiles recalled him saying beforehand that he didn't care what else FDR said, as long as he told the people the only thing they had to fear was fear — a rare glimpse of a speechwriter knowing he'd found the line.

author.name: Franklin D. Roosevelt
author.heading: About Franklin D. Roosevelt
author.bio: Franklin Delano Roosevelt (1882–1945) was the 32nd U.S. President and the only one elected to four terms, leading the nation through the Great Depression and most of World War II. The “fear itself” sentence was drafted for his 1933 inaugural by Louis McHenry Howe (1871–1936), his closest political adviser — FDR made it immortal in the delivery.
